activities.anchor: Printed as a book of single letters
activities.caption: call the magnitude — your genome in print
activities.name: dhVolumesEstimate

config.prompt: Your whole set of instructions — your genome — is about 3 billion rungs. Printed as a book of single letters, roughly how many volumes would it fill?
config.why: About a thousand volumes — spread across 23 pairs of chromosomes, holding roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.
config.context: And every one of your ~30 trillion cells runs on a copy of the same library.

activities.anchor: stretched out straight, would run about
activities.caption: fill the blanks — packing the library
activities.name: dhPackCloze

config.text: Your DNA in one cell, stretched out straight, would run about %%0%%. So it is packed, wound around spool-like proteins, into %%1%% chromosomes — %%2%% matched pairs, one of each pair from each parent. A full double set like this is called %%3%%.
config.hint: Think of the packing: two metres of ladder into a nucleus.

activities.anchor: Alternative versions of the same gene
activities.caption: pair each word with what it names
activities.name: dhTermsMatch

config.prompt: Three words this lesson needs used correctly — pair them:

pairs.right: a section of DNA coding for one protein, at a fixed address
an alternative version of the same gene — brown-eye vs blue-eye
one compact spool of wound DNA
a full double set — 23 matched pairs

config.why: Both chromosomes of a pair carry the same address, so you hold two copies of most genes — and the two copies may not be the same version.

activities.anchor: Reading the library goes like this
activities.caption: rebuild the reading scheme
activities.name: dhCodeOrder

config.prompt: From alphabet to working machinery — put the reading scheme in order:
items: The four bases are an alphabet
Three letters at a time spell one amino acid
Chains of amino acids fold into proteins
The proteins do the cell's work
config.why: The same reading scheme runs in bacteria, blue whales and bread wheat — the strongest single clue that everything alive shares one ancestor.

activities.anchor: about one letter per few hundred
activities.caption: true or false — copying the library
activities.name: dhRepJudge

statements.s: Replication is semi-conservative: each new ladder keeps one old strand and builds one new one.
statements.why: Confirmed by Meselson and Stahl's famous 1958 experiment.

statements.s: Copying is completely error-free; mutations come only from mutagens.
statements.why: Errors slip through spontaneously — about one letter per few hundred million copied — and most are caught and repaired.

statements.s: The rare escapee errors are mutations — the raw material of both disease and evolution.
statements.why: Mostly noise, occasionally signal — which is what evolution edits.

statements.s: Mitosis hands each new cell a single half-set of the library.
statements.why: Mitosis copies the full, unchanged double set — for growth and repair. Halving is meiosis's job.

activities.anchor: Making children has a counting problem
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the counting problem
activities.name: dhMeiosisSpot

config.prompt: This inheritance answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Each child gets one chromosome of every pair from each parent.
If parents handed over full double sets, the count would double every generation.
46 chromosomes would become 92, then 184 — nonsense within a century.
So gametes are made by ordinary mitosis, carrying a full double set of 46.
Fertilisation puts two single sets back together into 46.
config.correction: Gametes are made by MEIOSIS — a special two-stage division carrying a single set of 23.
config.why: Mitosis copies the full library; meiosis is the halving step that keeps the chromosome count constant across generations.

activities.caption: file the traits by their inheritance pattern
activities.name: dhTraitsBuckets

config.prompt: Not everything is a clean 3:1 — file each case:

items.label: an O allele — visible only in a double dose
blood groups A and B in one person — both shown
thousands of genes acting together, smooth ranges

config.why: A and B are codominant (an AB person shows both) while O is recessive; height and skin tone are polygenic — which is why Mendel's peas were, in a sense, lucky clean choices.

activities.anchor: changes the DNA your children will inherit
activities.caption: trace the mutation — who inherits it?
activities.name: dhMutationBranch

config.root: A mutation just happened. Only its address decides whether it stops with you or reaches your children.

choices.label: In a sunburnt skin cell
choices.feedback: Mutagen damage — UV light in sunlight.

choices.label: In a gamete
choices.feedback: Sperm and eggs carry a single set — and their mutations travel.

choices.label: In DNA that is repaired before the cell divides
choices.feedback: Most copying errors are caught and repaired.

skin.text: The mutation can turn that cell cancerous — but it dies with the skin. Your lineage is untouched.

germ.text: This one can reach the next generation — the germline is the only road inheritance runs on.

fixed.text: About one letter per few hundred million escapes — the rare escapees are mutations.

config.why: Only mutations in the gametes — or the germline cells that make them — pass to children: the distinction radiation safety, cancer medicine and evolution all depend on.
